extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IPR practitioners, and PTAB judges/administrative patent judges
extracted.subtask_description: Drafting an opposition to a Patent Owner’s Request for Discretionary Denial of Institution under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d) in an inter partes review before the PTAB, applying the Advanced Bionics framework, Director’s Memorandum factors, and related PTAB and Federal Circuit authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced Bionics two-part test for discretionary denial under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board uses a two-part test: (1) whether the same or substantially the same art or arguments were previously presented to the Office; and, if the first part is met, (2) whether the petitioner has shown that the Office erred in a material way with respect to patentability. Advanced Bionics, IPR2019-01469, Paper 6 at 7-8 (PTAB Feb. 13, 2020) (precedential).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the two prongs in sequence. If the asserted art/arguments are not the same or substantially the same as prosecution materials, discretionary denial under §325(d) is unlikely. If they are the same or substantially the same, evaluate whether the petitioner has demonstrated material error by the Office (see factors and examples below). The brief cites and relies on Advanced Bionics as controlling framework and treats related PTAB decisions as instructive precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (a): similarities and material differences between asserted art and prior art in examination
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) [T]he similarities and material differences between the asserted art and the prior art involved during examination;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to guide the first prong of Advanced Bionics: show whether the petition's references are meaningfully different from those before the Examiner. Emphasize distinguishing features (e.g., different disclosure of key claim limitations) to defeat the first-prong match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (b): cumulative nature of the asserted art and the prior art evaluated during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: (b) the cumulative nature of the asserted art and the prior art evaluated during examination;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also guides the first prong: if the asserted art is merely cumulative of what the Examiner had, that supports discretionary denial; if it supplies non-cumulative, distinct teachings, that supports institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (c): extent to which asserted art was evaluated during examination (including whether prior art was basis for rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: (c) the extent to which the asserted art was evaluated during examination, including whether the prior art was the basis for rejection;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides the second prong of Advanced Bionics: if the asserted art was not substantively considered or never formed the basis of a rejection, a petitioner can show the Office erred materially by overlooking it. Cite prosecution silence or lack of discussion to support material error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (d): extent of overlap between arguments in examination and petition reliance/owner distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: (d) the extent of the overlap between the arguments made during examination and the manner in which Petitioner relies on the prior art or Patent Owner distinguishes the prior art;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides the first prong: show whether petition repeats the same arguments made (and rejected/considered) in prosecution. Demonstrate meaningful new argumentation, new emphases, or new combinations to avoid being treated as duplicative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (e): whether Petitioner has pointed out sufficiently how the Examiner erred in its evaluation of the asserted prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: (e) whether Petitioner has pointed out sufficiently how the Examiner erred in its evaluation of the asserted prior art;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides the second prong: the petition must identify specific, persuasive errors (e.g., mischaracterizations by Applicant, overlooked teachings, failure to appreciate translations or appendices). Provide evidence (e.g., expert declarations, translations, documents) showing Examiner misapprehension or oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor (f): extent to which additional evidence/facts in the petition warrant reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: (f) the extent to which additional evidence and facts presented in the Petition warrant reconsideration of the prior art or arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides the second prong: show that documents or evidence not before the Examiner (or not considered in context) meaningfully affect patentability. If critical teaching was never before the Examiner, the petition need not rely on purely cumulative additional evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s Memorandum non-exhaustive considerations for discretionary denial
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Acting Director’s March 26, 2025 Memorandum (“Director’s Memo”), the PTAB outlined a non-exhaustive list of relevant considerations for discretionary denial including: 1. Whether the PTAB or another forum has already adjudicated the validity or patentability of the challenged patent claims; 2. Whether there have been changes in the law or new judicial precedent issued since issuance of the claims that may affect patentability; 3. The strength of the unpatentability challenge; 4. The extent of the petition’s reliance on expert testimony; 5. Settled expectations of the parties, such as the length of time the claims have been in force; 6. Compelling economic, public health, or national security interests; and 7. Any other considerations bearing on the Director’s discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this list as non-exhaustive; address each relevant item where helpful. For example, explain whether previous forum decisions exist, whether law has changed, the strength of the challenge (including evidentiary basis), the role of experts, whether parties’ expectations are truly 'settled', and whether public-interest factors weigh for or against denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material error example: misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of relevant prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: "An example of a material error may include misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of the relevant prior art where those teachings impact patentability of the challenged claims." (Advanced Bionics, Paper 6 at 8.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show concrete instances where Examiner missed or misinterpreted teachings (e.g., untranslated protocols or appendices, specific dose disclosures). Use expert declarations and primary-source evidence to demonstrate the oversight and connect it to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence in prosecution record can support a finding of Examiner error
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has recognized that 'if the record of the Office’s previous consideration of the art is not well developed or silent, then a petitioner may show the Office erred by overlooking something persuasive under factors (e) and (f).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prosecution is 'silent' as to a material reference (e.g., the reference was merely listed on an IDS and not discussed), emphasize that silence to argue the Examiner did not appreciate the reference and thereby materially erred. Cite PTAB cases (Amazon v. Nokia; Klein Tools) where silence supported institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDS volume/inundation can obscure material references and weigh against discretionary denial
rubrics_metrics.description: To inundate the Examiner with a large volume of prior art [] may obscure a single reference that is material and thus may be effectively as improper as withholding a material reference. (Ex Parte Morning Surf cited.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Patent Owner submitted hundreds or thousands of references in IDSs, argue that such volume could have obscured key references and that mere citation on an IDS is insufficient to show the Examiner considered or relied on them. Use PTAB decisions (Fellowes; Ecto World) as supporting precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence admissibility/procedural timing: 37 C.F.R. § 42.64(b) for translation certification objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to evidence (e.g., missing certified translation) should be made within 10 business days of institution, which then allows submission of translation certification as supplemental evidence within 10 business days of the timely filed objection. See 37 C.F.R. § 42.64(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on a non-English prosecution document, note whether a certified translation was submitted during prosecution; if not, a petitioner can supply a certified translation with the petition and the Patent Owner has a limited window to object. Cite the regulation and procedural timing when addressing evidentiary challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether asserted art formed the basis of a rejection (substantive consideration) matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the asserted art was evaluated during examination, including whether the prior art was the basis for rejection (Factor (c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reference was merely cited on an IDS and never used as the basis of a rejection or discussed in the file, argue that the Examiner did not evaluate it. Demonstrate that lack of substantive consideration supports institution under Advanced Bionics second prong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness sub-criteria: motivation to combine, reasonable expectation of success, and teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: Key obviousness considerations cited throughout include: (1) whether there was a motivation to combine the references; (2) whether there was a reasonable expectation of success; and (3) whether the prior art teaches away (or unexpected results exist). KSR principles apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing obviousness or responding to prosecution arguments, address these sub-criteria explicitly: show why a POSA would be motivated to combine (medical need, prior art problem-solution), why expectation of success is reasonable (prior art disclosures, clinical practice, dose adjustability), and whether purported teaching away or unexpected results are supported by contemporaneous evidence or rebutted by later literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindsight assessment guidance: focus on whether a POSA would have seen a benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper question is not 'whether a [POSA] writing on a blank slate would necessarily have chosen [the claimed approach]' but whether he or she 'would have seen a benefit' to modifying the teachings of the asserted art to achieve the claimed invention (citing KSR and Janssen decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allegations of impermissible hindsight by tying the reasoning to contemporaneous motivations, known problems in the field, or evidence that research was being pursued. Show that POSAs had reasons to try the claimed modifications at the relevant time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settled expectations factor is contextual and does not rest solely on Patent Owner’s R&D investment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director’s Memo contemplates 'settled expectations of the parties, such as the length of time the claims have been in force.' The brief argues that a patent owner’s assertion of its own settled expectation (e.g., R&D investment) is insufficient alone to warrant discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When opposing or supporting discretionary denial, analyze the timing (how long the patent has been in force), whether challengers delayed, and whether expectations truly are 'settled' (market reliance, long issuance), rather than relying solely on self-serving statements about investment. For recent patents and prompt petitions, argue settled expectations weigh against denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest/economic-health considerations may favor institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Compelling economic and public health interests (Director’s Memo item) are relevant; failure to consider the merits may run counter to these interests—e.g., preventing higher drug costs by allowing review of obvious treatment patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address whether institution would serve public health or economic interests (e.g., access to cheaper therapeutics). Use authoritative sources (clinical guidelines, NCCN, trials) to show public-interest weight for institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert testimony: quantify and contextualize reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Director’s Memo factor 4: 'The extent of the petition’s reliance on expert testimony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the petition relies heavily on expert declarations, explain the basis, persuasiveness, and corroborating documentary evidence. If Patent Owner criticizes reliance on experts, show that experts interpret primary art and explain technical significance, especially where prosecution record lacks discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat untranslated or partially disclosed prosecution documents as potentially not considered
rubrics_metrics.description: References identified on IDSs but submitted untranslated (or without certified translation) or not expressly discussed in prosecution may not have been substantively considered by the Examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that absence of an English translation in prosecution and lack of discussion in remarks/rejections indicates the Examiner did not appreciate the material teachings; supply certified translations and explain how translated content alters the prosecution-picture materially.
